label: lem:order-taylor
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:order-taylor}
Let $f\in\mathfrak m^d$ and $w=(w_1,\ldots,w_n)\in\mathfrak m^qR^n$, where $q\ge1$.  Then
\[
 f(x+tw)-f(x)-t\sum_iw_i\partial_i f
 \in\mathfrak m^{d+2(q-1)}k[[t,x]].
\]
Consequently, if
$\sum_iw_i\partial_i f\in\mathfrak m^{N+1}$ and $d+2(q-1)\ge N+1$, then
$x\mapsto x+tw$ fixes $j^Nf$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to consider a monomial $x^\alpha$ of total degree
$s=|\alpha|\ge d$.  Expanding gives
$(x+tw)^\alpha =\sum_{\beta\le\alpha} \binom{\alpha}{\beta}x^{\alpha-\beta}t^{|\beta|}w^\beta$.
The terms with $|\beta|=0$ and $|\beta|=1$ are respectively
$x^\alpha$ and $t\sum_iw_i\partial_i(x^\alpha)$.  If
$r=|\beta|\ge2$, then
$x^{\alpha-\beta}\in\mathfrak m^{s-r}$ and $w^\beta\in\mathfrak m^{rq}$, so the
corresponding term has $\mathfrak m$-order at least
$(s-r)+rq=s+r(q-1)\ge d+2(q-1)$.
Summing over the monomials of $f$ proves the first assertion.\\

Under the additional hypotheses, both the linear term and the remainder lie
in $\mathfrak m^{N+1}k[[t,x]]$, hence
$f(x+tw)\equiv f(x)\pmod{\mathfrak m^{N+1}}$.  Finally $q\ge1$, so the linear part
in $x$ of $x\mapsto x+tw$ has matrix $I+tA$, whose determinant has constant
term $1$.  Thus the substitution is an automorphism over $k[[t]]$.
head: environment

label: thm:smooth
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:smooth}
Let $f$ be isolated, $d=\operatorname{ord}(f)$, and $\eta=\eta(f)$.  For every $N\ge2\eta-d-1$, the scheme-theoretic stabilizer $H_N\subseteq\mathcal R_N$, that is, the closed subgroup scheme
representing $N$-jet coordinate changes that fix $j^Nf$, is smooth.
Consequently the orbit map is separable and
\[
 T_{j^Nf}(\mathcal R_N\cdot j^Nf)
 =\frac{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)+\mathfrak m^{N+1}}{\mathfrak m^{N+1}}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $v\in\mathfrak m R^n$ represent a tangent vector to $H_N$, so
$\delta(v)=\sum_i v_i\partial_i f\in\mathfrak m^{N+1}$.  The numerical hypothesis and
$\eta\ge d$ imply $N\ge\eta-1$.  Hence
$\mathfrak m^{N+1} =\mathfrak m^{N+1-\eta}\mathfrak m^\eta \subseteq\mathfrak m^{N+1-\eta}\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f) =\mathfrak m^{N+2-\eta}\operatorname{Jac}(f)$.
Choose $w\in\mathfrak m^qR^n$, where $q=N+2-\eta\ge1$, such that
$\delta(w)=\delta(v)$, and put $z=v-w$.  Then $\delta(z)=0$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:integrate} gives a stabilizer arc $\alpha_z(t)$ with tangent
vector $z$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:order-taylor} gives a stabilizer arc
$\alpha_w(t):x\mapsto x+tw$, because
$d+2(q-1)=d+2(N+1-\eta)\ge N+1$.
Their composition $\alpha_z(t)\circ\alpha_w(t)$ is a $k[[t]]$-valued point of the
scheme-theoretic stabilizer $H_N$ and has tangent vector $z+w=v$ modulo
$\mathfrak m^{N+1}$.  Thus every tangent vector of $H_N$ is represented by a formal arc in $H_N$.\\

Since $\operatorname{Spec} k[[t]]$ is reduced, every morphism
$\operatorname{Spec} k[[t]]\to H_N$ factors uniquely through the reduction
$(H_N)_{\mathrm{red}}$.  Consequently every tangent vector of $H_N$ lies in
$T_e(H_N)_{\mathrm{red}}$; the reverse inclusion is tautological, and hence
\[
 T_eH_N=T_e(H_N)_{\mathrm{red}}.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:standard-inputs}\ref{std:group}, $(H_N)_{\mathrm{red}}$ is smooth.  The
reduction has the same underlying topological space as $H_N$, so
\[
 \dim_kT_eH_N
 =\dim_kT_e(H_N)_{\mathrm{red}}
 =\dim_e(H_N)_{\mathrm{red}}
 =\dim_eH_N.
\]
Thus the local ring of $H_N$ at the identity has embedding dimension equal to its Krull
dimension and is regular.  Since $k$ is perfect, regularity of this finite-type group scheme at
the identity implies smoothness there; translations by group-valued points then give smoothness
everywhere.  Finally $\mathcal R_N$ is smooth, and the orbit dimension formula yields
\[
 \operatorname{rank}(d_eo_{f,N})
 =\dim\mathcal R_N-\dim H_N
 =\dim(\mathcal R_N\cdot j^Nf).
\]
The differential is therefore onto the tangent space of the orbit, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:standard-inputs}\ref{std:sep} gives separability.
head: environment

label: cor:mu-sep
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:mu-sep}
If $\mu(f)=\mu$, then $\mathfrak m^\mu\subseteq \operatorname{Jac}(f)$, hence
$\mathfrak m^{\mu+1}\subseteq\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)$ and $\eta(f)\le\mu+1$.  Consequently every
$N\ge2\mu-1$ is a separable level; in particular every $N\ge2\mu$ is
simultaneously sufficiently large for right determinacy and separability.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Artin local algebra $\frac{R}{\operatorname{Jac}(f)}$ has length $\mu$, so its maximal ideal has
$\mu$-th power zero.  The rest follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:smooth} and
$d\ge2$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Greuel--Pham observed that contact orbit maps may be inseparable in positive
characteristic, but reported that no nonseparable example was known for the right group
when the hypersurface singularity is isolated \cite[Section~5]{GreuelPham2020}.
Theorem~\ref{thm:smooth} shows that such an example cannot occur in sufficiently high
jet order: every isolated hypersurface singularity has separable right orbit maps from
the explicit level $N\ge2\eta(f)-\operatorname{ord}(f)-1$ onward.
head: environment

label: cor:smooth-stabilizers-arbitrary-field
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:smooth-stabilizers-arbitrary-field}
Let $K$ be any field of positive characteristic, and let
$f\in\mathfrak m^2\subseteq K[[x_1,\ldots,x_n]]$ have finite
Milnor number. Put $d=\operatorname{ord}(f)$ and
$\eta=\min\{a\ge1:\mathfrak m^a\subseteq\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)\}$. Then the scheme-theoretic stabilizer of $j^Nf$ in the
right jet group is smooth over $K$ whenever $N\ge\max\{1,2\eta-d-1\}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Extend scalars to an algebraic closure $\overline K$.
The containment $\mathfrak m^\eta\subseteq\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)$ persists
in $\overline K[[x]]$, so the extended germ remains
isolated and its corresponding exponent is at most
$\eta$. Its order remains $d$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:smooth} therefore makes the
base-changed stabilizer smooth over $\overline K$.
Stabilizers for the finite jet action commute with
field extension, and smoothness descends under the
faithfully flat extension $K\subseteq\overline K$.
head: environment

label: def:Fmod
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:Fmod}
For an isolated germ $f$, put
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 Q_F(f)&=S\cap\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f),\\
 A_F(f)&=\frac{S}{Q_F(f)},\\
 \operatorname{Fmod}(f)&=\dim_k\left(\frac{\mathfrak n_F}{Q_F(f)}\right)
 =\operatorname{length}_k\left(A_F(f)\right)-1.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The \emph{Frobenius type} is the $\operatorname{Aut}_k(S)$-orbit of $Q_F(f)$.
head: environment

label: prop:Fbasic
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Fbasic}
The algebra $A_F(f)$, its Frobenius type, and $\operatorname{Fmod}(f)$ are invariant under
right equivalence.  Moreover $\operatorname{Fmod}(f)<\infty$ if and only if $f$ is
isolated.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $g=\varphi(f)$ with $\varphi\in\mathcal R$, the chain rule and invertibility of the
Jacobian matrix of $\varphi$ give $\operatorname{Jac}(g)=\varphi(\operatorname{Jac}(f))$.  Also $\varphi(S)=S$ and
$\varphi(\mathfrak n_F)=\mathfrak n_F$, since $S$ is the common kernel of the derivations.  Hence
$Q_F(g)=\varphi(Q_F(f))$.\\

If $f$ is isolated, choose $a$ with $\mathfrak m^a\subseteq \operatorname{Jac}(f)$.  For $pr\ge a+1$,
$\mathfrak n_F^r\subseteq\mathfrak m^{pr}\subseteq\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)$, so $A_F(f)$ has finite length.
Conversely, if $\mathfrak n_F^r\subseteq Q_F(f)$, then
$\langle x_1^p,\ldots,x_n^p\rangle^r\subseteq\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)$.  For a monomial
$x^\alpha$ write $\alpha_i=pq_i+r_i$ with $0\le r_i<p$.  If
$\sum_iq_i\le r-1$, then $|\alpha|\le p(r-1)+n(p-1)$.  Hence
$\mathfrak m^{p(r-1)+n(p-1)+1}\subseteq\langle x_1^p,\ldots,x_n^p\rangle^r\subseteq\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)\subseteq \operatorname{Jac}(f)$,
so $\operatorname{Jac}(f)$ is $\mathfrak m$-primary.  This argument does not presuppose isolatedness.
head: environment

label: prop:Flower
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Flower}
For every isolated $f$, one has $\operatorname{Fmod}(f)\le\operatorname{pmod}(f)$ and $\operatorname{Fmod}(f)\le\operatorname{Rmod}(f)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $d=\operatorname{Fmod}(f)$ and choose polynomial representatives
$h_1,\ldots,h_d\in\mathfrak n_F$ whose classes form a basis of $\frac{\mathfrak n_F}{Q_F(f)}$.
Put $V=\operatorname{Span}_k\{h_1,\ldots,h_d\}$.  Then $V\cap\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)=0$.  For
$g_t=f+\sum_a t_ah_a$, all first derivatives of the $h_a$ vanish, so
$\operatorname{Jac}(g_t)=\operatorname{Jac}(f)$ and $\mu(g_t)=\mu(f)$.\\

Choose $N$ sufficiently large that $\mathfrak m^{N+1}\subseteq\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)$, all $h_a$
survive in $\mathcal J_N$, right determinacy holds, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:smooth} applies uniformly to the family.  The affine
parameter space has tangent space $j^NV$, whereas the orbit tangent space at
every member is
$\frac{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)+\mathfrak m^{N+1}}{\mathfrak m^{N+1}}$.  These spaces meet trivially.  Hence a
positive-dimensional right-equivalence fiber would have a smooth point with
a nonzero tangent vector in their intersection, a contradiction.  Thus the
general right-equivalence fiber is zero-dimensional, giving
$d\le\operatorname{Rmod}(f)$.\\

The same directions occur in a semiuniversal unfolding with trivial section,
and the corresponding $d$-plane is $\mu$-constant.  Hence
$d\le\operatorname{pmod}(f)$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Set
\[
 \varepsilon_F(f)=
 \operatorname{length}_R\left(\frac{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)}{Q_F(f)R}\right),
 \qquad
 \gamma_p(f)=
 \dim_k\left(\frac{R}{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)+\langle x_1^p,\ldots,x_n^p\rangle}\right).
\]
By the Nakayama lemma, $\gamma_p(f)$ is the minimal number of generators of
$M_f=\frac{R}{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)}$ as an $A_F(f)$-module; this is why we call it the generator number.
head: environment

label: thm:length
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The ring $R$ is free of rank $p^n$ over $S$, with basis
$x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}$, $0\le a_i<p$.  Hence
$\dim_k\left(\frac{R}{Q_F(f)R}\right)=p^n(d+1)$.
The exact sequence
$0\to\frac{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)}{Q_F(f)R}\to\frac{R}{Q_F(f)R}\to\frac{R}{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)}\to0$
and
$0\to\frac{\operatorname{Jac}(f)}{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)}\to\frac{R}{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)}\to\frac{R}{\operatorname{Jac}(f)}\to0$
give \eqref{eq:exact-length}, since
$\dim_k\left(\frac{\operatorname{Jac}(f)}{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)}\right)=n$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:regular}.\\

Furthermore
$Q_F(f)=\operatorname{Ann}_S(M_f)$,
because an element of $S$ annihilates $M_f$ exactly when it kills $[1]$.
Thus $M_f$ is a finite $A_F(f)$-module, minimally generated by
$\gamma_p(f)$ elements.  Nakayama gives a surjection
$A_F(f)^{\gamma_p(f)}\twoheadrightarrow M_f$, whence
$\mu(f)+n\le\gamma_p(f)(d+1)$.
Finally $\frac{M_f}{\mathfrak n_F M_f}$ is a quotient of
$\frac{R}{\langle x_1^p,\ldots,x_n^p\rangle}$, so $\gamma_p(f)\le p^n$.
head: environment

label: cor:equality
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:equality}
Equality $\mu(f)+n=\gamma_p(f)(\operatorname{Fmod}(f)+1)$ holds exactly when $M_f$ is free over
$A_F(f)$ of rank $\gamma_p(f)$.  Equality
$\mu(f)+n=p^n(\operatorname{Fmod}(f)+1)$ holds exactly when $\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)=Q_F(f)R$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first assertion follows because the surjection
$A_F(f)^{\gamma_p(f)}\twoheadrightarrow M_f$ is an isomorphism exactly when the
finite lengths agree.  The second follows from the kernel
$\frac{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)}{Q_F(f)R}$ of $\frac{R}{Q_F(f)R}\twoheadrightarrow\frac{R}{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)}$.
head: environment

label: prop:Fimage
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Fimage}
The Frobenius map on $M_f$ satisfies $\operatorname{ima} F\cong A_F(f)$ and $\operatorname{Fmod}(f)+1=\dim_k\operatorname{ima} F$.  If $b_e(f)=\dim_k\operatorname{ima} F^e$, then $\operatorname{Rmod}(f)\ge b_e(f)-1$, $b_1(f)\ge b_2(f)\ge\cdots\ge1$, and $b_e(f)=1$ for $e\gg0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The image of Frobenius on $R$ is $S$, and the kernel of $S\to M_f$ is
$Q_F(f)$.  Replacing $p$ by $p^e$ in the argument of
Proposition~\ref{prop:Flower} gives $\operatorname{Rmod}(f)\ge b_e(f)-1$.  The images
are nested, and a sufficiently high Frobenius power kills the maximal ideal
of the Artin algebra $M_f$.
head: environment

label: thm:Ftower
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:Ftower}
For every $e\ge1$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $A_e\cong\operatorname{ima} F^e$ and $p^{en}b_e=\mu(f)+n+\varepsilon_e(f)$.
\item $\mu(f)+n\le\gamma_e(f)b_e$ and $\gamma_e(f)\le p^{en}$.
\item $\operatorname{Rmod}(f)\ge b_e-1$ and $\operatorname{pmod}(f)\ge b_e-1$.
\item $b_1\ge b_2\ge\cdots\ge1$, and $b_e=1$ for $e\gg0$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof is identical to that of Theorem~\ref{thm:length}, replacing $S$
by $S_e$ and $p^n$ by $p^{en}$.  The nonconstant elements of $S_e$ have
zero first derivatives, so the same Frobenius-slice argument gives both
modality inequalities.
head: environment

label: def:Frobenius-Loewy-length
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:Frobenius-Loewy-length}
The \emph{Loewy length} of a local Artin algebra $(A,\mathfrak q)$ is the least integer
$\ell\ge1$ such that $\mathfrak q^\ell=0$.  We denote the Loewy length of $A_F(f)$ by
$\ell_F(f)=\min\{\ell\ge1\mid\mathfrak n_F^\ell\subseteq Q_F(f)\}$ and put
$B_F(f)=p(\ell_F(f)-1)+n(p-1)$.
head: environment

label: lem:loewy
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The middle containments are immediate.  Write a monomial exponent as
$\alpha_i=pq_i+r_i$, $0\le r_i<p$.  If
$\sum_iq_i\le\ell_F(f)-1$, then
$|\alpha|\le p(\ell_F(f)-1)+n(p-1)=B_F(f)$.
Thus every monomial of degree at least $B_F(f)+1$ lies in
$\langle x_1^p,\ldots,x_n^p\rangle^{\ell_F(f)}$.
head: environment

label: thm:eta-radius
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:eta-radius}
Let $f\in\mathfrak m^2$ be isolated and set  $N_\eta(f)=2\eta(f)-\operatorname{ord}(f)$. Then
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $f$ is right $N_\eta(f)$-determined;
\item every right orbit map at level
      $N\ge N_\eta(f)-1$ is separable;
\item the $k[[t]]$-algebra
      \[
         M_{N_\eta(f)}(f)
         =\frac{R}{\mathfrak m^{N_\eta(f)}\operatorname{Jac}(f)}
      \]
      is a complete right-equivalence invariant.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently,
\[
   2B_F(f)-\operatorname{ord}(f)+2
\]
is also a right classification radius.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since
$\mathfrak m^{\eta(f)}\subseteq\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)$, we have that $\mathfrak m^{\eta(f)+1}\subseteq\mathfrak m^2\operatorname{Jac}(f)$, and so from Lemma~\ref{lem:standard-inputs}\ref{std:det} we have that $f$ is right $(2\eta-d)$-determined. In addition, Assertion \textup{(ii)} is Theorem~\ref{thm:smooth}. Finally, for $d_J=\operatorname{ord}(\operatorname{Jac}(f))\ge1$ we have that 
\[
   \left\lfloor\frac{N_\eta(f)+\operatorname{ord}(f)+d_J+1}{2}\right\rfloor
   =
   \eta(f)+\left\lfloor\frac{d_J+1}{2}\right\rfloor
   \ge\eta(f)+1.
\]
Thus the hypothesis of
Lemma~\ref{lem:standard-inputs}\ref{std:MY} holds,
proving \textup{(iii)}.
Finally $\eta\le B_F(f)+1$ gives the stated
Frobenius-Loewy radius.
head: environment

label: cor:lowmodideal
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:lowmodideal}
If $r=\operatorname{Rmod}(f)$, then
\[
 \langle x_1^p,\ldots,x_n^p\rangle^{r+1}\subseteq\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f),\qquad
 \eta(f)\le pr+n(p-1)+1.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\operatorname{Fmod}(f)\le r$, the maximal ideal of $A_F(f)$ has $(r+1)$-st power
zero.  Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:loewy}.
head: environment

label: prop:lowtypes
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:lowtypes}
Up to $\operatorname{Aut}_k(S)$, every colength-$(d+1)$ ideal $Q\subseteq S$ for
$d\le3$ has one of the following forms, with undisplayed variables killed
linearly:
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
d&Q\\ \hline
0&\langle y_1,\ldots,y_n\rangle,\\[1mm]
1&\langle y_2,\ldots,y_n,y_1^2\rangle,\\[1mm]
2&\langle y_2,\ldots,y_n,y_1^3\rangle,\\
 &\langle y_3,\ldots,y_n\rangle+\langle y_1,y_2\rangle^2,\\[1mm]
3&\langle y_2,\ldots,y_n,y_1^4\rangle,\\
 &\langle y_3,\ldots,y_n,y_1y_2,y_2^2,y_1^3\rangle,\\
 &\langle y_3,\ldots,y_n,y_1^2,y_2^2\rangle,\\
 &\langle y_4,\ldots,y_n\rangle+\langle y_1,y_2,y_3\rangle^2.
\end{array}
\]
In characteristic $2$ there is in addition the nonalternating
$(1,2,1)$ type
\[
 \langle y_3,\ldots,y_n,y_1y_2,y_1^2+y_2^2\rangle.
\]
Only types realized as $S\cap\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)$ occur for hypersurface germs.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The possible Hilbert functions of a local Artin algebra of length at most
four are $(1)$, $(1,1)$, $(1,1,1)$, $(1,2)$, $(1,1,1,1)$, $(1,2,1)$, and
$(1,3)$.  All cases except $(1,2,1)$ follow by choosing a generator in each nonzero graded
piece and lifting a basis of the embedding space.  In the remaining case multiplication
induces, after choosing a generator of the one-dimensional vector space $\mathfrak q^2$, a
nonzero symmetric bilinear form on the two-dimensional vector space
$\frac{\mathfrak q}{\mathfrak q^2}$.  Changing generators acts by congruence and rescaling the
socle rescales the form.  Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic different
from $2$, the form has rank $1$ or $2$.  In characteristic $2$, the nondegenerate case
has two congruence types, alternating and nonalternating.  Writing normal forms for these
bilinear forms gives exactly the displayed ideals.
head: environment

label: prop:Fmod-zero-criterion
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The local algebra $A_F(f)=\frac{S}{Q_F(f)}$ has length one exactly when $Q_F(f)=\mathfrak n_F$.
Since $\mathfrak n_F=\langle x_1^p,\ldots,x_n^p\rangle S$, this is equivalent to (iii).
Because $k$ is perfect, (iii) is equivalent to (iv).
The remaining assertions follow from Lemma~\ref{lem:loewy},
Theorem~\ref{thm:eta-radius}, and Theorem~\ref{thm:length}.
head: environment

label: thm:Fmod-zero-classification
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:Fmod-zero-classification}
The jet map induces a bijection
\[
 \frac{\{f\in\mathfrak m^2\mid\operatorname{Fmod}(f)=0\}}{\!\overset{\mathcal R}{\sim}}
 \ \longrightarrow
 \frac{\mathcal Z_{n,p}}{\mathcal R_N},
 \qquad N=2n(p-1).
\]
Equivalently, every such germ is right equivalent to a polynomial of degree
at most $N$, and two such germs are right equivalent exactly when their
$N$-jets lie in the same $\mathcal R_N$-orbit.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The forward implication follows from
Proposition~\ref{prop:Fmod-zero-criterion}.  Conversely let
$u\in\mathcal Z_{n,p}$ and let $f$ be a lift.  Since
$\mathfrak m^{B+1}\subseteq\langle x_1^p,\ldots,x_n^p\rangle$,
the defining condition gives
$\mathfrak m^{B+1}\subseteq\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)+\mathfrak m^{2B+1}$.
Set
$L=\frac{\mathfrak m^{B+1}+\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)}{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)}$.
Because $\mathfrak m^{2B+1}=\mathfrak m^B\mathfrak m^{B+1}$, the preceding inclusion implies
$L\subseteq\mathfrak m^B L\subseteq\mathfrak m L$.  Since also $\mathfrak m L\subseteq L$, we obtain
$L=\mathfrak m L$, and the Nakayama lemma gives $L=0$.  Hence
$\mathfrak m^{B+1}\subseteq\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)$ and therefore
$\mathfrak m^{2B+1}\subseteq\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)$.  The congruences defining
$\mathcal Z_{n,p}$ consequently become exact:
$x_i^p\in\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)$.  Thus $\operatorname{Fmod}(f)=0$. Theorem~\ref{thm:eta-radius} makes every such germ right $N$-determined, so
right equivalence is exactly the $\mathcal R_N$-orbit relation on $N$-jets.
head: environment

label: cor:Fmod-zero-explicit
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:Fmod-zero-explicit}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*]
\item If $n=1$, the isolated germs $f$ with $\operatorname{Fmod}(f)=0$ are exactly
$x^d$, up to right equivalence, with $2\le d\le p-1$.
\item If $p=2$, an isolated germ $f$ has $\operatorname{Fmod}(f)=0$ if and only if $n$ is even
and
$f\overset{\mathcal R}{\sim} x_1x_2+x_3x_4+\cdots+x_{n-1}x_n$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $n=1$, write $f=\sum_{j\ge2}a_jx^j$.  Since $f$ is isolated, there is a
least $d$ such that $a_d\ne0$ and $p\nmid d$, and then $\operatorname{Jac}(f)=\langle x^{d-1}\rangle$ up to a unit,
so $\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)=\langle x^d\rangle$.  The image of $k[[x^p]]$ in $\frac{R}{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)}$ has basis
$1,x^p,x^{2p},\ldots,x^{\left\lfloor\frac{d-1}{p}\right\rfloor p}$.  Hence
$\operatorname{Fmod}(f)=\left\lfloor\frac{d-1}{p}\right\rfloor$.  Thus $\operatorname{Fmod}(f)=0$ forces $d\le p$, and since
$p\nmid d$ we have $d\le p-1$.  There is then no positive multiple of $p$ below $d$,
so $d=\operatorname{ord}(f)$ and $f=x^du(x)$ with $u(0)\ne0$.  Because $p\nmid d$, the unit
$u$ has a $d$-th root in $k[[x]]$, giving $f\overset{\mathcal R}{\sim} x^d$.\\

For $p=2$, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:standard-inputs}\ref{std:split}:
$f\overset{\mathcal R}{\sim} g(x_1,\ldots,x_c)+q$.  Put
$\mathfrak m_g=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_c\rangle\subseteq k[[x_1,\ldots,x_c]]$.  Suspension invariance gives
$\operatorname{Fmod}(g)=0$.  If $c>0$, then $\operatorname{Jac}(g)\subseteq\mathfrak m_g^2$, so
$\mathfrak m_g\operatorname{Jac}(g)\subseteq\mathfrak m_g^3$, contradicting
$x_i^2\in\mathfrak m_g\operatorname{Jac}(g)$.
Thus $c=0$, and the remaining nonsingular quadratic form is hyperbolic over
the algebraically closed field $k$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
For $p\ge5$, isolated homogeneous cubics $f$ in three variables have
$\operatorname{Fmod}(f)=0$ but may have positive right modality.  Indeed their three
quadratic partial derivatives form a regular sequence, so the Jacobian
algebra has socle degree $3$, hence $\mathfrak m^4\subseteq \operatorname{Jac}(f)$ and
$\mathfrak m^5\subseteq\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)$.  Since $p\ge5$, one has $x_i^p\in\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)$.
Thus $\operatorname{Fmod}(f)=0$ is not equivalent to right simplicity.
head: environment

label: prop:persistence
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:persistence}
For every isolated $f$,
\[
 \operatorname{Rmod}(f)\ge d_0(f)\ge d_1(f)\ge\cdots\ge\operatorname{Fmod}(f),
\qquad
 d_0(f)\le\operatorname{pmod}(f).
\]
If $d(f)=\operatorname{ord}(\operatorname{Jac}(f))$ and $B_F=B_F(f)$, then
\[
 d_r(f)=\operatorname{Fmod}(f)\qquad
 r\ge\max\{0,B_F-d(f)\}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The inclusions
$\mathcal P_{r+1}\subseteq\mathcal P_r$ and
$S\cap\mathfrak m\subseteq\mathcal P_r$ give monotonicity and the lower Frobenius
bound.  Choose independent classes represented by
$h_1,\ldots,h_e\in\mathcal P_r$.  Write the gradient of $h_a$ as
$A_a(\partial_1f,\ldots,\partial_nf)^{\mathsf T}$ with $A_a\in M_n(\mathfrak m^r)$.  For
$g_t=f+\sum_at_ah_a$, its gradient is obtained from $(\partial_1f,\ldots,\partial_nf)^{\mathsf T}$ by
multiplication with $I+\sum_at_aA_a$.  This matrix is invertible on a neighborhood
of the origin in parameter space,
so $\operatorname{Jac}(g_t)=\operatorname{Jac}(f)$.  The same finite-jet transversality argument as in
Proposition~\ref{prop:Flower} gives $e\le\operatorname{Rmod}(f)$, and for $r=0$ the
family is $\mu$-constant, giving $e\le\operatorname{pmod}(f)$.\\

If $r+d(f)\ge B_F$, then every partial derivative of
$h\in\mathcal P_r$ lies in $\mathfrak m^{B_F}$.  Consider a monomial $c x^\alpha$ occurring in $h$ with
total degree at most $B_F$.  If some $\alpha_i$ is not divisible by $p$, then its image
under $\partial_i$ is a nonzero monomial of degree $<B_F$; distinct monomials of $h$
cannot cancel after applying the same $\partial_i$.  Thus every exponent of every such
monomial is divisible by $p$.  Since $k$ is perfect, the truncation of $h$ through degree
$B_F$ lies in $S$.  Therefore
$h=s+u$ with $s\in S\cap\mathfrak m$ and $u\in\mathfrak m^{B_F+1}$.  By
Lemma~\ref{lem:loewy}, $u\in\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)$.  Thus every surviving class is represented
by a Frobenius direction.
head: environment

label: prop:susp
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The partial derivatives of the nonsingular quadratic block generate the quadratic
variables.  Every nonconstant $p$-th-power monomial involving one of those variables
therefore belongs to $\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)$, while setting the quadratic variables equal to zero
maps $\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)$ onto $\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(g)$.
head: environment

label: lem:char2-corank
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:char2-corank}
Assume $p=2$, and let $g$ be an isolated residual germ
in $c$ variables. Then we have that 
$\operatorname{Rmod}(g)\ge c+\binom c3$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The assertion is immediate for $c=0$. Assume $c>0$.
Let $V_2^{\mathrm{sq}}=\operatorname{Span}_k\{x_1^2,\ldots,x_c^2\}$ and $V_3=k[x_1,\ldots,x_c]_3$. Since $\operatorname{Hess}(g)(0)=0$, its quadratic part belongs to
$V_2^{\mathrm{sq}}$. Consider the unfolding $g+h_2+h_3$ for $(h_2,h_3)\in V_2^{\mathrm{sq}}\oplus V_3$. Its parameter-to-$3$-jet map is injective, and the
parameter space has dimension $c+\binom{c+2}{3}$.\\

Write a coordinate change as $\varphi(x)=Ax+u(x)$ with
$u\in\mathfrak m^2k[[x]]^c$. In characteristic two, substituting
$\varphi$ into a square quadratic form produces no cubic
contribution from $u$. Substitution into a cubic form
affects its cubic part only through $A$.
Consequently the action on the $3$-jets in this family
factors through $\operatorname{GL}_c$.\\

Every right-equivalence fiber in the parameter space is
therefore contained in a $\operatorname{GL}_c$-orbit at the $3$-jet
level, and has dimension at most $c^2$.
After restricting to a neighborhood of the origin where
the fibers are isolated, the relative modality is at least $c+\binom{c+2}{3}-c^2=c+\binom c3$. The modality of an unfolding is at most the right
modality of its central germ, proving the assertion.
head: environment

label: thm:uniform
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $p\ne2$, the residual germ has order at least three, and
\cite[Proposition~2.18]{GreuelNguyen2016} gives
$\operatorname{Rmod}(g)\ge\binom{c+\operatorname{ord}(g)-1}{\operatorname{ord}(g)}-c^2\ge\binom c3$.
For $p=2$ use Lemma~\ref{lem:char2-corank}.  Thus $c\le C_{p,D}$ in all
characteristics.\\

The Milnor bound follows from \eqref{eq:essential-bound} and
$\operatorname{Fmod}(g)\le\operatorname{Rmod}(g)\le D$.  Theorem~\ref{thm:eta-radius}, applied in $c$ variables, gives the radius $2pD+2c(p-1)\le N_{p,D}$.\\

Finally, Corollary~\ref{cor:order} applied to $g$ gives
\[
 D+1\ge
 \binom{c+\left\lceil\frac{\operatorname{ord}(g)}{p}\right\rceil-1}{c}.
\]
For $c>0$, the right-hand side is at least
$\left\lceil\frac{\operatorname{ord}(g)}{p}\right\rceil$, proving $\operatorname{ord}(g)\le p(D+1)$.
head: environment

label: cor:uniform-full-determinacy
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:uniform-full-determinacy}
Fix $p>0$ and $D\ge0$.  Every isolated hypersurface germ $f$ with
$\operatorname{Rmod}(f)\le D$ is right $\widehat N_{p,D}$-determined, independently of the
number of ambient variables.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $f\overset{\mathcal R}{\sim} g(x_1,\ldots,x_c)+Q(z_1,\ldots,z_{n-c})$ as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:standard-inputs}\ref{std:split}.  If $c=0$, the germ is a nonsingular quadratic form and is right
$2$-determined.  Assume $c>0$ and put
$B=p(\ell_F(f)-1)+c(p-1)=B_F(g)$.  Since
$\ell_F(f)-1\le\operatorname{Fmod}(f)\le D$ and $c\le C_{p,D}$, one has
$B\le B_{p,D}$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:loewy}, applied to the residual germ, gives
$\mathfrak m_x^{B+2}\subseteq\mathfrak m_x^2\operatorname{Jac}(g)$.  On the other hand the partial derivatives of the
nonsingular quadratic form $Q$ generate the ideal
$\langle z_1,\ldots,z_{n-c}\rangle$.  Since $B\ge1$, every monomial of total
degree at least $B+2$ that involves a split variable belongs to
$\mathfrak m^2\langle z_1,\ldots,z_{n-c}\rangle$.  Therefore, in the full power-series
ring,
\[
 \mathfrak m^{B+2}\subseteq\mathfrak m^2\operatorname{Jac}(f).
\]

Lemma~\ref{lem:standard-inputs}\ref{std:det} shows that $f$ is
right $(2B-\operatorname{ord}(f)+2)$-determined, hence right $2B$-determined
because $\operatorname{ord}(f)\ge2$. Since
$2B\le N_{p,D}\le\widehat N_{p,D}$, the assertion follows.
head: environment

label: cor:stable-milnor-growth
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:stable-milnor-growth}
Let $r=\operatorname{Rmod}(f)$.  Then
\[
 \mu(f)\le p^{\,2+\sqrt[3]{6r}}(r+1).
\]
Consequently, for fixed $p$, any sequence $(f_j)$ of isolated hypersurface singularities with
$\mu(f_j)\to\infty$ has $\operatorname{Rmod}(f_j)\to\infty$, even if the ambient dimension is allowed to
tend to infinity.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The definition of $C_{p,r}$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:char2-corank} imply
$\binom c3\le r$ for the residual essential corank in every characteristic.  Hence
$c(c-1)(c-2)\le6r$ and therefore $c\le2+\sqrt[3]{6r}$.  Apply
\eqref{eq:essential-bound} and $\operatorname{Fmod}(f)\le r$.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Fix $p>0$.  If $\{f_j\}_{j=1}^\infty$ is any sequence of isolated hypersurface singularities in
characteristic $p$ with $\mu(f_j)\to\infty$, then
$\operatorname{Rmod}(f_j)\to\infty$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: This is immediate from Corollary~\ref{cor:stable-milnor-growth}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Nguyen proved that $\mu(f)\le4p$ for singularities of right modality at most two
\cite[Corollary~3.7]{Nguyen2019}.  Corollary~\ref{cor:stable-milnor-growth} gives an analogous
bounded-Milnor-number statement in every finite modality and, moreover, makes the bound
independent of the ambient dimension.  This is compatible with the broader finiteness
phenomenon conjectured by Greuel--Nguyen for singularities with an arbitrary number of
moduli \cite{GreuelNguyen2016}.
head: environment

label: cor:order
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:order}
If $r=\operatorname{ord}(f)$, then
\[
 \operatorname{Fmod}(f)\ge
 \binom{n+\left\lceil\frac{r}{p}\right\rceil-1}{n}-1.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)\subseteq\mathfrak m^r$,
$Q_F(f)\subseteq S\cap\mathfrak m^r =\mathfrak n_F^{\left\lceil\frac{r}{p}\right\rceil}$.
Compare colengths.
head: environment

label: prop:BP
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:BP}
Let $f=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_i}$ with $p\nmid a_i$, and put $b_i=a_i-1$.  Then
\[
 \operatorname{Fmod}(f)+1=
 \prod_{i=1}^n
 \left\lceil\frac{b_i}{p}\right\rceil
 +\#\{i\mid p\mid b_i\}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Up to units,
$\operatorname{Jac}(f)=\langle x_1^{b_1},\ldots,x_n^{b_n}\rangle$.  The monomials outside $\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)$ are those
with every exponent strictly below the corresponding $b_i$, together with the
exceptional pure monomials $x_i^{b_i}$.  Intersecting this set with the
$p$-lattice gives the stated count.
head: environment

label: thm:pmodlower
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:pmodlower}
For every isolated $f$, one has $\operatorname{pmod}(f)\le\operatorname{Rmod}(f)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $\mu=\mu(f)$ and choose an irreducible component
$C\subseteq\mathcal C_\mu(F)$ through $0$ of dimension $\operatorname{pmod}(f)$.
Take $N\ge2\mu$ sufficiently large.  By
Corollary~\ref{cor:mu-sep}, every $\mu$-constant member has separable
$N$-jet orbit, and the orbit tangent space has constant codimension
$\mu+n-1$.  At the origin the semiuniversal parameter space is complementary
to this tangent space; hence transversality persists on a dense open subset
of $C$.\\

A positive-dimensional right-equivalence fiber would have a smooth point with
a nonzero tangent vector lying both in the parameter tangent space and in the
orbit tangent space.  This contradicts transversality.  Hence the general
right-equivalence fiber on $C$ is zero-dimensional, and right-completeness
gives
$\operatorname{Rmod}(f)\ge\dim C=\operatorname{pmod}(f)$.
head: environment

label: lem:lambda-qe
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:lambda-qe}
For every closed point $x\in X$, $\lambda(x)=\iota e_\pi(x)$.  Moreover, $\iota$ is a
power of $p$ dividing $M$, and every local Milnor number on the critical cover is
divisible by $\iota$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $y=\pi(x)$ and let
$A=\mathcal O_{Y,y}^{\mathrm{sh}}$
be the strict henselization, with fraction field $F$.  Since $\pi$ is finite
flat,
$X_A=X\times_Y\operatorname{Spec} A$
is finite flat over $A$.  Because $A$ is strictly henselian, $X_A$ decomposes
into the local factors corresponding to the points of the geometric fiber.
Let $B_x$ be the factor corresponding to $x$.  Its rank is the local special
fiber length:
$\operatorname{rank}_A B_x=\lambda(x)$.\\

Since $Y$ is normal, $A$ is a normal local domain, and
$\frac{F}{k(Y)}$ is separable algebraic.  Thus separable base change preserves the
inseparable degree of $\frac{k(X)}{k(Y)}$.  The generic algebra
$B_x\otimes_AF$
is a finite product of fields $L_1,\ldots,L_s$, and every $\frac{L_j}{F}$ has
inseparable degree $\iota$.  Hence
$\lambda(x) =\dim_F(B_x\otimes_AF) =\sum_j[L_j:F] =\iota\sum_j[L_j:F]_{\mathrm{sep}}$.
By the preceding étale-local definition of local degree, the last sum is
$e_\pi(x)$.
Therefore $\lambda(x)=\iota\,e_\pi(x)$.\\

Finally
$M=[k(X):k(Y)] =\iota[k(X):k(Y)]_{\mathrm{sep}}$,
so $\iota$ is a power of $p$ dividing $M$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The local degree used here is the algebro-geometric local number of sheets of a finite
map.  Gaffney--Lazarsfeld used this invariant to study higher ramification loci of finite
coverings \cite{GaffneyLazarsfeld1980}; the form and semicontinuity statements used
above are developed in the thesis of Lazarsfeld \cite{Lazarsfeld1980Thesis}.  The factor
$\iota=[k(X):k(Y)]_{\mathrm{insep}}$ is the extra positive-characteristic thickness that is
absent for a generically separable complex covering.
head: environment

label: prop:critical-length-pmod
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:critical-length-pmod}
After shrinking $X$ around $x_0$, the following holds for every closed point $x\in X$. Put $h=G_x$ and $m=\mu(h)=\lambda(x)>0$. Then
\[
\operatorname{codim}_{X,x}\Lambda_{\ge m}=m-1-\operatorname{pmod}(h).
\]
Equivalently, $\dim_x\Lambda_{\ge m}=M+n-m+\operatorname{pmod}(h)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose $N\ge2M$ and put
$E_N=\frac{\mathfrak m^2}{\mathfrak m^{N+1}}$
in the $y$-variables.  For $v\in E_N$ choose a lift $\widetilde v$ and set
$\mu_N(v)= \dim_k \left(\frac{k[[y]]}{\operatorname{Jac}(\widetilde v)+\mathfrak m^{M+1}}\right)$.
Changing the lift changes its partial derivatives only by elements of
$\mathfrak m^N\subseteq\mathfrak m^{M+1}$, so $\mu_N$ is well defined.\\

Suppose $\mu_N(v)=m\le M$.  The maximal ideal of the Artin algebra
$\frac{k[[y]]}{\operatorname{Jac}(\widetilde v)+\mathfrak m^{M+1}}$
has $m$-th power zero, so
$\mathfrak m^m\subseteq \operatorname{Jac}(\widetilde v)+\mathfrak m^{M+1}$.
Put
\[
 L_v=\frac{\mathfrak m^m+\operatorname{Jac}(\widetilde v)}{\operatorname{Jac}(\widetilde v)}.
\]
Modulo $\operatorname{Jac}(\widetilde v)$, the inclusion $\mathfrak m^m\subseteq\operatorname{Jac}(\widetilde v)+\mathfrak m^{M+1}$ gives $L_v\subseteq \mathfrak m^{M+1-m}L_v$. Since $m\le M$, one has $M+1-m\ge1$, and therefore $L_v\subseteq\mathfrak m L_v$. Nakayama's lemma gives $L_v=0$.
Thus $\mathfrak m^m\subseteq \operatorname{Jac}(\widetilde v)$, and therefore
$\mathfrak m^{M+1}\subseteq \operatorname{Jac}(\widetilde v)$.  Consequently
$\mu(\widetilde v)=\mu_N(v)=m$.
The converse is immediate.  Hence
$\mathcal M_m=\{v\in E_N\mid\mu_N(v)=m\}$
is exactly the Milnor-number-$m$ locus and is a locally closed determinantal
subset.\\

At $h$ one has
$T_h= \frac{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(h)}{\mathfrak m^{N+1}} \subseteq E_N, \qquad \dim_k\left(\frac{E_N}{T_h}\right) =\dim_k\left(\frac{\mathfrak m^2}{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(h)}\right) =m-1$.
Choose a linear complement $V$ to $T_h$.  A basis of $V$, together with
$y_1,\ldots,y_n$, gives a basis of $\frac{\mathfrak m}{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(h)}$, so
$h+\sum_i a_i y_i+v,\qquad v\in V$,
is semiuniversal with trivial section.  For $m>0$, its Milnor-number-$m$ locus is
contained in $a=0$.  Therefore
$\dim_0\{v\in V\mid\mu(h+v)=m\} =\operatorname{pmod}(h)$.\\

The map
$\Theta: \mathcal R_N\times(j^Nh+V)\to E_N, \qquad (\varphi,j^Nh+v)\mapsto\varphi(j^Nh+v)$
has surjective differential at $(e,j^Nh)$ because the group directions give
$T_h$ and $V$ gives a complement.  Thus $\Theta$ is smooth there.  Since
right equivalence preserves Milnor number,
$\operatorname{codim}_{E_N,j^Nh}\mathcal M_m =m-1-\operatorname{pmod}(h)$.\\

Now let
$\Phi:X\to E_N,\qquad z\mapsto j^NG_z$.
In the original critical-incidence coordinates,
$D_j= \frac{\partial G}{\partial t_j} = h_j(u+y)-h_j(u) -\sum_i\partial_i h_j(u)y_i$.
At $x_0$ these classes form a basis of
$\frac{\mathfrak m^2}{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)}$.  Consider the finite relative module
$\mathcal E_N=\frac{\langle y_1,\ldots,y_n\rangle^2}{\langle y_1,\ldots,y_n\rangle \operatorname{Jac}_y(G)+\langle y_1,\ldots,y_n\rangle^{N+1}}$.
The cokernel of the sections $D_1,\ldots,D_{M-1}$ vanishes at $x_0$ and
therefore vanishes after shrinking $X$.  Every local fiber length is at most
the total rank $M$, hence $\mu(G_z)\le M$ and
$\langle y_1,\ldots,y_n\rangle^{N+1}\subseteq\langle y_1,\ldots,y_n\rangle \operatorname{Jac}(G_z)$.  Thus the fiber of $\mathcal E_N$ at
$z$ is exactly
$\frac{\mathfrak m^2}{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(G_z)}$.
It follows that the critical-family directions surject onto
$\frac{E_N}{T_{G_z}}$.\\

Therefore
$\Psi: \mathcal R_N\times X\to E_N,\qquad (\varphi,z)\mapsto\varphi(\Phi(z))$
is smooth at $(e,x)$.  Smooth base change preserves local codimension, so
$\operatorname{codim}_{X,x} \{z\mid\mu(G_z)=m\} =m-1-\operatorname{pmod}(h)$.
Finally $\lambda$ is upper semicontinuous and $\lambda(x)=m$, so after
shrinking around $x$ there are no points with $\lambda\ge m+1$.  Hence the
exact-$m$ locus agrees locally with $\Lambda_{\ge m}$.
head: environment

label: lem:rosenlicht-to-pmod
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:rosenlicht-to-pmod}
Let $Y$ be irreducible and suppose the family has constant Milnor number $m>0$.  If the
general right-equivalence fiber has dimension $i$, then a general member $g$ satisfies
$\operatorname{pmod}(g)\ge\dim Y-i$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a general member $g$ and a jet level $N\ge2m$ sufficiently high for
right determinacy and separability.  Let
$T_g= T_{j^Ng}(\mathcal R_N\cdot j^Ng)$
and choose a linear complement
$\mathcal J_N=T_g\oplus U$.
Then
$\dim U=m+n-1$.
The action map
$\Theta: \mathcal R_N\times(j^Ng+U)\to \mathcal J_N$
is smooth at $(e,j^Ng)$.\\

Form the fiber product, using $\iota_N:Y\to \mathcal J_N$ and the action map $\Theta$,
$Z=Y\times_{\mathcal J_N}\bigl(\mathcal R_N\times(j^Ng+U)\bigr)$
near the point lying over $g$.  The projection $Z\to Y$ is a base change of
$\Theta$, hence smooth of relative dimension
$\rho= \dim\mathcal R_N+\dim U-\dim \mathcal J_N$.
Since the orbit codimension is $m+n-1=\dim U$, one has
$\rho=\dim\operatorname{Stab}_{\mathcal R_N}(j^Ng)$, and this stabilizer dimension
is constant on the Milnor-number-$m$ locus.\\

Consider the projection
$\sigma:Z\to U$.
For fixed $u$, the image in $Y$ of a fiber of $\sigma$ lies in a single
right-equivalence fiber, whose general dimension is at most $i$.
For fixed $u$ and a fixed member of that right-equivalence fiber, the choices
of the group element form a stabilizer coset of dimension $\rho$.
Hence the general fiber of $\sigma$ has dimension at most $i+\rho$.
Therefore
$\dim\overline{\sigma(Z)} \ge \dim Z-(i+\rho) = \dim Y-i$.\\

Every $j^Ng+u$ occurring in $\sigma(Z)$ is right equivalent to a member of
$Y$, hence has Milnor number $m$.  Shrink the slice $g+U$ around $g$ so that
$\mu\le m$, which is possible by upper semicontinuity.  On the other hand the condition
$\mu\ge m$ is closed on the finite jet space (it is a determinantal rank condition), so
the closure of $\sigma(Z)$ in this neighborhood is still $m$-constant.  It contains
$0\in U$ in its closure.  Consequently
$\operatorname{pmod}(g)\ge\dim\overline{\sigma(Z)}\ge\dim Y-i$.
head: environment

label: lem:lazarsfeld-purity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:lazarsfeld-purity}
Let $\pi:X\to Y$ be a finite surjective morphism of smooth integral varieties and let
$x_0\in X$.  Write $d=e_\pi(x_0)$.  After replacing $X$ and $Y$ by sufficiently small
neighborhoods of $x_0$ and $\pi(x_0)$, the following holds.  If $T\subseteq X$ is an
irreducible subvariety through $x_0$ whose generic local degree $e_\pi(T)$ is strictly less
than $d$, then there is an irreducible codimension-one subvariety $T_1\subseteq T$ through
$x_0$ with
\[
 e_\pi(T_1)>e_\pi(T).
\]
Consequently, if $e_\pi(T)\ge e_0$, then there is an irreducible
$T^*\subseteq T$ through $x_0$ with generic local degree $d$ and
\[
 \operatorname{codim}_T(T^*)\le d-e_0.
\]
head: environment
name: Higher purity for local degree

title: Proof
body_md:
The codimension-one increase is the local form of the higher-purity theorem of Lazarsfeld
\cite[Theorem~2.2 and statement~(2.4)]{Lazarsfeld1980Thesis}.  Iterating it, the generic
local degree increases by at least one at each step and can never exceed $d$.  Starting from
a generic degree at least $e_0$, at most $d-e_0$ steps are required.
head: environment

label: thm:pmod-rmod-general
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:pmod-rmod-general}
For every isolated hypersurface singularity over an algebraically closed field
of characteristic $p>0$,
\[
 \operatorname{pmod}(f)=\operatorname{Rmod}(f).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Theorem~\ref{thm:pmodlower} gives
$\operatorname{pmod}(f)\le\operatorname{Rmod}(f)$.  Put $r=\operatorname{Rmod}(f)$ and assume $r>0$.\\

Use the semiuniversal unfolding
$F(x;a,t)=H(x,t)+\sum_i a_ix_i$
introduced above.  By the Rosenlicht parameter-count description of modality,
there is an irreducible locally closed subset $Y_0$ of the parameter space,
with $0\in\overline{Y_0}$, such that the general right-equivalence fiber on
$Y_0$ has dimension $i$ and
$\dim Y_0-i=r$.
Replacing $Y_0$ by a dense open subset, we may suppose that its Milnor number
is constant, say $m$.  Since $r>0$, one must have $m>0$. This is true since  Since $\dim Y_0-i=r>0$, the general member of $Y_0$ cannot be smooth, because all smooth germs form a single right-equivalence class. Thus $m>0$. In the chosen semiuniversal coordinates, $\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_i}(0;a,t)=a_i$. Hence every parameter value with $a\ne0$ gives a smooth germ. The dense Milnor-number-$m$ part of $Y_0$ is therefore contained in the linear subspace $a=0$; after replacing $Y_0$ by this dense open subset, we may assume $a=0$ identically on $Y_0$.\\

By Lemma~\ref{lem:rosenlicht-to-pmod}, for a general member $g$ of $Y_0$,
$\operatorname{pmod}(g)\ge r$.\\

Because $a=0$, the point $u=0$ is a critical point of every member of
$Y_0$.  Thus the dense Milnor-number-$m$ part of $Y_0$ has a canonical lift to
the critical incidence space.  Pull this lifted set through the étale
localization defining $X$, and choose an irreducible component $Z$ whose
closure contains $x_0$.  For general $z\in Z$,
$\lambda(z)=m,\qquad \operatorname{pmod}(G_z)\ge r$.
Put
$D=M+n-m+r$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:critical-length-pmod} gives
$\dim_z\Lambda_{\ge m}\ge D$
for general $z\in Z$.\\

After shrinking around $x_0$, write
$\Lambda_{\ge m}=S_1\cup\cdots\cup S_N$
as its irreducible decomposition.  The union of those $S_j$ of dimension at
least $D$ contains a dense open subset of $Z$, hence contains $Z$.  Since
$Z$ is irreducible, it lies in one such component, say $S$.  Thus
$x_0\in S,\qquad \dim S\ge M+n-m+r$.\\

Let
$\iota=[k(X):k(Y)]_{\mathrm{insep}}$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:lambda-qe},
$e_\pi(x_0)=\frac{M}{\iota},\qquad e_\pi(S)\ge\frac{m}{\iota}$.
Since $e_\pi(S)\ge\frac{m}{\iota}$ and
$e_\pi(x_0)=\frac{M}{\iota}$, Lemma~\ref{lem:lazarsfeld-purity} produces an irreducible
subvariety $S^*\subseteq S$ through $x_0$ with generic local degree
$\frac{M}{\iota}$ and
\[
 \operatorname{codim}_S(S^*)\le\frac{M-m}{\iota}.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:lambda-qe}, the generic local length on $S^*$ is therefore $M$.
Since $\Lambda_{\ge M}$ is closed, $S^*\subseteq\Lambda_{\ge M}$, and
\[
 \dim S^*\ge M+n-m+r-\frac{M-m}{\iota}.\\
\]

Applying Proposition~\ref{prop:critical-length-pmod} at $x_0$ gives
$\dim_{x_0}\Lambda_{\ge M} =n+\operatorname{pmod}(f)$.
Consequently
$\operatorname{pmod}(f) \ge r+(M-m)\left(1-\frac{1}{\iota}\right) \ge r =\operatorname{Rmod}(f)$.
Together with the reverse inequality already proved, this gives $\operatorname{pmod}(f)=\operatorname{Rmod}(f)$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Gabrielov proved equality of modality and proper modality for isolated complex analytic
hypersurface singularities \cite{Gabrielov1974}.  In positive characteristic, Nguyen
proved the equality for univariate germs \cite{Nguyen2014} and for all germs of right
modality at most two \cite{Nguyen2019}; in the latter paper the general equality was
formulated as Conjecture~2.2.  Theorem~\ref{thm:pmod-rmod-general} proves that
conjecture for arbitrary isolated hypersurface singularities.
head: environment

label: cor:insep-forces-pmod
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:insep-forces-pmod}
With $\iota$ as above,
\[
 \operatorname{pmod}(f)=\operatorname{Rmod}(f)
 \ge
 \mu(f)\left(1-\frac{1}{\iota}\right).
\]
If $p\nmid\mu(f)$, then $\iota=1$.  If $p=2$ and $n$ is odd, then
$\iota\ge2$ and
\[
 \operatorname{pmod}(f)=\operatorname{Rmod}(f)\ge\frac{\mu(f)}{2}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\lambda=\iota e_\pi$ and $M=\mu(f)$,
$\Lambda_{\ge M} = R_{\frac{M}{\iota}-1}(\pi)$
in Lazarsfeld notation.  His Theorem~2.2 gives
$\operatorname{codim}_{X,x_0} \Lambda_{\ge M} \le\frac{M}{\iota}-1$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:critical-length-pmod} gives
$\operatorname{codim}_{X,x_0} \Lambda_{\ge M} =M-1-\operatorname{pmod}(f)$,
which proves the inequality. Since $\iota$ is a power of $p$ dividing $M$, the condition $p\nmid M$ forces
$\iota=1$.  In characteristic $2$, the Hessian in the $x$-variables has zero diagonal and is
alternating.  The Jacobian matrix of the critical map $\Pi$ is block triangular, with
this Hessian (up to sign) as its $u$-block and an identity matrix in the $t$-block.
If $n$ is odd, the Hessian determinant vanishes identically, so $d\Pi$ is not generically
of full rank.  Since $\Pi$ is finite dominant, it is generically inseparable and
$\iota\ge2$.
head: environment

label: cor:char2-odd-corank
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:char2-odd-corank}
Assume $p=2$ and let $c=c(f)$ be odd.  Then
\[
 \operatorname{Rmod}(f)\ge\frac{\mu(f)}{2}\ge2^{c-1}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Split off the nonsingular quadratic part and let $g$ be the residual germ in $c$
variables.  Suspension invariance gives $\mu(g)=\mu(f)$ and
$\operatorname{Rmod}(g)=\operatorname{Rmod}(f)$.  Since $c$ is odd, Corollary~\ref{cor:insep-forces-pmod}
applied to $g$ gives $\operatorname{Rmod}(g)\ge\frac{\mu(g)}{2}$.  For a residual germ in
characteristic two one has $\operatorname{Jac}(g)\subseteq\mathfrak m_x^2$.  The Jacobian ideal is an
$\mathfrak m_x$-primary parameter ideal in the regular local ring $k[[x_1,\ldots,x_c]]$;
hence its colength equals its Hilbert--Samuel multiplicity.  Monotonicity of
multiplicity under inclusion gives
$\mu(g)=e(\operatorname{Jac}(g))\ge e(\mathfrak m_x^2)=2^c$.  Combining the two inequalities proves the
claim.
head: environment

label: prop:rmod-upper
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:rmod-upper}
Every isolated hypersurface germ satisfies $\operatorname{pmod}(f)=\operatorname{Rmod}(f)\le\mu(f)-1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a basis
$x_1,\ldots,x_n,h_1,\ldots,h_{\mu-1}$
of $\frac{\mathfrak m}{\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)}$ with $h_j\in\mathfrak m^2$.  A nonzero linear parameter in the
corresponding semiuniversal unfolding makes the germ smooth, and all smooth
germs form one right orbit.  Hence every positive-dimensional quotient is
contained in the $(\mu-1)$-dimensional subspace on which the linear
parameters vanish.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
If $n=1$, then we have that $\operatorname{Fmod}(f)=\operatorname{pmod}(f)=\operatorname{Rmod}(f)
 =\left\lfloor\frac{\mu(f)}{p}\right\rfloor$. This is true since the right-modality formula is the univariate classification of Nguyen
\cite{Nguyen2014} and the Frobenius formula follows from the fact that
$\mathfrak m\operatorname{Jac}(f)=\langle x^{\mu+1}\rangle$, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:pmod-rmod-general} identifies proper and right modality.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let an algebraic group $G$ act on a variety $X$.  A locally closed subvariety
$T\subseteq X$ is \emph{orbit-finite} if every $G$-orbit meets $T$ in finitely many
points.  Thus the parameters are genuine moduli up to a finite ambiguity; this is the
finite-fiber notion usually called a \emph{modular family} in singularity classification.
A finite collection of such subvarieties is a \emph{finite modular atlas} for an
invariant constructible subset if every orbit meets at least one of them.
head: environment

label: lem:finite-modular-principle
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:finite-modular-principle}
Let an algebraic group $G$ act on a variety $X$, and let $W\subseteq X$ be invariant and
constructible with $G$-modality at most $D$.  Then $W$ admits a finite modular atlas
$T_1,\ldots,T_s$ with $\dim T_i\le D$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a Rosenlicht stratification and reduce to a geometric quotient
$q:V\to Y$ with $V\subseteq W$ and $V,Y$ irreducible.  The definition of modality gives
$\dim Y\le D$.\\

The generic fiber $V_{k(Y)}$ has a closed point whose residue field is finite over
$k(Y)$.  The closure $T$ of that point in $V$ is dominant and generically finite over
$Y$.  After shrinking $Y$ it is quasi-finite and surjective, so it meets every orbit
over that open set in finitely many points.  Apply the same construction over the
complement.  Noetherian induction terminates, and repeating this on the finitely many
Rosenlicht pieces proves the claim.
head: environment

label: lem:stable-cancellation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:stable-cancellation}
Let $g\in\mathfrak m_c^2$ and $h\in\mathfrak m_d^2$ be residual germs, so that neither has a
nonsingular quadratic summand.  If $g$ and $h$ are stably right equivalent, then
$c=d$ and $g\overset{\mathcal R}{\sim}h$.
head: environment
name: Cancellation of nonsingular quadratic suspensions

title: Proof
body_md:
By stable right equivalence there are nonsingular quadratic forms $Q$ and $\widetilde Q$ such
that $g+Q\overset{\mathcal R}{\sim}h+\widetilde Q$.  The uniqueness statement in
Lemma~\ref{lem:standard-inputs}\ref{std:split} identifies the residual parts of
right-equivalent germs, also in characteristic $2$; see \cite{GreuelPfister2026}.  Hence the residual variable counts agree and the
residual germs are right equivalent.
head: environment

label: thm:finite-modular-classification
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $M=M_{p,D}$ and choose
$L\ge\max\{2M,M+1,N_{p,D}\}$.  The residual corank $c=0$ contributes one stable
class, represented by the zero residual germ; include it as a zero-dimensional family.
We may therefore assume $c\ge1$.  For each $1\le c\le C_{p,D}$ let
$E_{c,L}=\frac{\mathfrak m_c^2}{\mathfrak m_c^{L+1}}$ and let $\mathcal R_{c,L}$ be the algebraic right-jet group.\\

For a jet $v$ choose a lift $h$ and define $\mu_L(v)$ as the dimension of
$\frac{k[[x_1,\ldots,x_c]]}{\operatorname{Jac}(h)+\mathfrak m_c^{M+1}}$.  This is independent of the lift because
$L\ge M+1$.  The condition $\mu_L(v)\le M$ is determinantal and hence constructible.
If $\mu_L(v)=m\le M$, the maximal ideal of the length-$m$ truncated Jacobian algebra
has $m$-th power zero, so $\mathfrak m_c^m\subseteq \operatorname{Jac}(h)+\mathfrak m_c^{M+1}$.  The Nakayama lemma upgrades
this to $\mathfrak m_c^m\subseteq \operatorname{Jac}(h)$; hence the truncated length equals the actual Milnor
number.  The converse is immediate.\\

Intersect with the closed locus $\mathcal H_{c,L}$.  Since $L\ge2M$, every isolated germ
there is right $L$-determined, so its formal right modality is the modality of its
$L$-jet.  Upper semicontinuity of modality for algebraic group actions
\cite[Proposition~2.7]{GreuelNguyen2016} makes the locus $W_{c,D}$ of modality at
most $D$ invariant and constructible.\\

Theorem~\ref{thm:uniform} shows that every stable class with modality at most $D$ has a
residual representative in one of the finitely many $W_{c,D}$.  Apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-modular-principle}.  The tautological $L$-jets over the resulting
orbit-finite multisections are algebraic polynomial families.  Since every fiber is
right $N_{p,D}$-determined, truncate to degree $N_{p,D}$.  This does not change the
represented formal orbit.  It also preserves orbit-finiteness: if two truncated
parameters lie in the same $N_{p,D}$-jet orbit, their corresponding formal germs are
right equivalent by $N_{p,D}$-determinacy.  Conversely, because all representatives
under consideration are residual, Lemma~\ref{lem:stable-cancellation} shows that two of
them represent the same stable class only if they are right equivalent.  Thus each
stable class occurs at only finitely many parameters on each multisection.  Finally
refine by the finitely many Milnor numbers and integer modality values.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Greuel--Nguyen observed that, for each fixed positive characteristic, only finitely many
right-simple singularities occur and conjectured an analogous finiteness phenomenon for
an arbitrary number of moduli \cite{GreuelNguyen2016}.  Nguyen subsequently gave
explicit finite lists of modular normal-form families in modalities one and two
\cite{Nguyen2019}.  Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-modular-classification} gives a stable,
finite-atlas form of this finiteness phenomenon in every modality.  Thus it also
realizes the general finiteness expectation stated in the introduction of
\cite{GreuelNguyen2016}.  It is a finite algebraic parametrization statement rather
than an explicit list of normal forms.  For a complementary ADE-type classification
over complete regular local rings, organized by Cohen--Macaulay type rather than right
modality, see \cite{SvorayADE2025}.
head: environment

label: cor:stable-finite-classification
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:stable-finite-classification}
For every fixed characteristic and finite modality bound, stable right classification is
a finite algebraic classification problem: finitely many modular families of dimension
at most the modality suffice.  In modality zero this gives finiteness of stable right-simple classes without using an explicit normal-form classification.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The Fedder criterion made Frobenius splitting of hypersurfaces computable
\cite{Fedder1983}.  Hara--Yoshida introduced generalized test ideals
\cite{HaraYoshida2003}, while Musta\c{t}\u{a}--Takagi--Watanabe introduced and
studied $F$-thresholds and related them to the jumping behavior of test ideals
\cite{MTW2005}.  Blickle--Musta\c{t}\u{a}--Smith proved discreteness and rationality
in the regular $F$-finite setting \cite{BMS2008}.  Musta\c{t}\u{a} then constructed
positive-characteristic Bernstein--Sato polynomials and related their roots to
$F$-jumping numbers \cite{Mustata2009}; Blickle--St\"abler extended this framework to
test modules \cite{StaeblerBS}.
head: environment

label: thm:fpt-modality
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:fpt-modality}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $\displaystyle \operatorname{fpt}(f)\ge\frac{1}{\max\{2,2B_F^{\mathrm{res}}\}}$.
\item If $c>0$, then $\displaystyle
\operatorname{fpt}(f)\ge\frac{1}{2B_F^{\mathrm{res}}}\ge\frac{1}{2pr+2c(p-1)}$.
\item If $c=0$, then $\operatorname{fpt}(f)=\frac{1}{2}$ in one variable and odd characteristic; if the
quadratic form contains a hyperbolic plane, then $\operatorname{fpt}(f)=1$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:eta-radius} to the residual germ $g$.  Since
$\ell_F(g)=\ell_F(f)$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:susp}, a right coordinate change in the
$x$-variables sends $g$ to a polynomial $g_{\le 2B_F^{\mathrm{res}}}$ of degree at most
$2B_F^{\mathrm{res}}$.  Extending that coordinate change trivially across the variables
of $Q$ shows that $f$ is right equivalent to
$g_{\le 2B_F^{\mathrm{res}}}+Q$, whose degree is at most
$\max\{2,2B_F^{\mathrm{res}}\}$.\\

If $h$ is a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $N$, put
$a=\left\lfloor\frac{q-1}{N}\right\rfloor$ for $q=p^e$.  Then $h^a$ is nonzero and has
total degree less than $q$, hence cannot lie in $\langle x_1^q,\ldots,x_n^q\rangle$.  Therefore
$\nu_e(h)\ge a$, and passage to the limit gives $\operatorname{fpt}(h)\ge\frac{1}{N}$.  This proves the
first bound.  If $c>0$, then $B_F^{\mathrm{res}}\ge c(p-1)\ge1$, so the maximum is
$2B_F^{\mathrm{res}}$; moreover
$\ell_F(f)-1\le\operatorname{Fmod}(f)\le r$, which gives the second bound.\\

If $c=0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:standard-inputs}\ref{std:split} leaves only the
nonsingular quadratic form.  Over an
algebraically closed field, a nonsingular quadratic form in at least two variables
contains a hyperbolic plane $uv$.  Then $Q^{q-1}$ contains the monomial
$u^{q-1}v^{q-1}$ with nonzero coefficient, so $\nu_e(Q)=q-1$ and $\operatorname{fpt}(Q)=1$.
The only remaining case is one variable in odd characteristic, where $Q$ is right
equivalent to $x^2$ and $\operatorname{fpt}(Q)=\frac{1}{2}$.
head: environment

label: prop:fpt-refined
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:fpt-refined}
If $c=c(f)$, then
\[
 \operatorname{fpt}(f)\ge
 \frac{1-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ord}(f)}}{p^c(\operatorname{Fmod}(f)+1)-c}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[Corollary~2.14]{Svoray2026},
$\operatorname{fpt}(f)\ge\frac{1}{\operatorname{Tj}(f)}\left(1-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ord}(f)}\right)$.  Since $\operatorname{Tj}(f)\le\mu(f)$, apply
\eqref{eq:essential-bound}.
head: environment

label: prop:Freg-new
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Freg-new}
Assume $p\nmid N$ and let $f_N=xy-z^N$.  Then $\frac{k[[x,y,z]]}{\langle f_N\rangle}$ is strongly
$F$-regular and $\operatorname{fpt}(f_N)=1$, whereas
$\operatorname{Fmod}(f_N)=\operatorname{pmod}(f_N)=\operatorname{Rmod}(f_N)=\left\lfloor\frac{N-1}{p}\right\rfloor$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The hyperbolic block $xy$ splits off, leaving $z^N$.  The univariate formula and
Theorem~\ref{thm:pmod-rmod-general} give the modality statement.  The ring is the tame
cyclic quotient $k[[u,v]]^{\boldsymbol{\mu}_N}$ for the action $\zeta\cdot(u,v)=(\zeta u,\zeta^{-1}v)$, with $x=u^N$, $y=v^N$, and $z=uv$.  Since $p\nmid N$,
the invariant ring is a direct summand of the regular ring and hence strongly
$F$-regular by \cite{HochsterHuneke1994}.  It is $F$-pure, so the principal
$F$-pure threshold is one.
head: environment

label: cor:uniform-m-adic-constancy
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first assertion is precisely Corollary~\ref{cor:uniform-full-determinacy}.  The
$F$-pure threshold and the set of $F$-jumping numbers are invariant under local
coordinate changes.  Generalized test ideals commute with local isomorphisms, localization, and completion in the regular $F$-finite setting \cite[Proposition~2.13]{BMS2008}; in particular they are functorial under ring automorphisms, which gives the displayed identity.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Hernández--Núñez-Betancourt--Witt proved local $\mathfrak m$-adic constancy of the
$F$-pure threshold and, with a deeper perturbation order, literal equality of all test
ideals $\tau(f^\lambda)$ for $0\le\lambda<1$ around a fixed polynomial with an
isolated singularity \cite{HNBW2018}.  Their explicit radii depend on the Jacobian
colength and the ambient dimension.  Corollary~\ref{cor:uniform-m-adic-constancy}
has a different form: its radius is uniform on the whole bounded-modality locus and is
independent of ambient dimension, while the test ideals are identified up to the
coordinate change supplied by right determinacy.
head: environment

label: thm:universal-Fjump-spectrum
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:universal-Fjump-spectrum}
If $f$ is isolated and $\operatorname{Rmod}(f)\le D$, then every $F$-jumping number of $\langle f\rangle$ in
$(0,1]$ belongs to the finite set $\Xi_{p,D}$.  Consequently only finitely many
numerical $F$-jumping spectra, and in particular only finitely many $F$-pure thresholds,
can occur at fixed $p,D$, independently of the original ambient dimension.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
After splitting, either the quadratic block contains a hyperbolic plane or it has
rank at most one.  Over an algebraically closed field the latter alternative can occur
only in odd characteristic. If the quadratic block contains no hyperbolic plane, then
it is zero in characteristic two and has dimension at most
one in odd characteristic. Hence, in the non-hyperbolic case,
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-modular-classification} reduces the germ to a principal
polynomial in at most $n_{p,D}=C+\delta_p$ variables and of degree at most
$d_{p,D}$.  Test ideals and their jumping numbers are unchanged by the local
coordinate changes used here and commute with localization and completion in this
regular $F$-finite setting; see \cite[Proposition~2.13]{BMS2008}.  Proposition~3.8 of
\cite{BMS2008}, with one generator, therefore puts every global $F$-jumping exponent of
this polynomial in the displayed finite denominator set.  A local jump at the maximal
ideal is necessarily a global jump: if the two adjacent test ideals become distinct
after localization at the maximal ideal, then they were already distinct before
localization.  Hence every local $F$-jumping number occurring here belongs to the same
finite denominator set.\\

If the quadratic block has rank at least two, it contains a hyperbolic plane $uv$;
by Lemma~\ref{lem:standard-inputs}\ref{std:split} the residual term $h$ involves
variables disjoint from $u,v$.  For
every $q=p^e$, the monomial $u^{q-1}v^{q-1}$ occurs with coefficient one in
$(h+uv)^{q-1}$ and cannot cancel.  Thus the hypersurface is $F$-pure and its first jump is $1$; there are no
jumps in $(0,1)$.
head: environment

label: cor:Fjump-separation
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every reduced denominator is at most $Q_{p,D}$.  Two distinct reduced fractions with
denominators at most $Q_{p,D}$ differ by at least $\frac{1}{Q_{p,D}^2}$.
head: environment

label: thm:one-level-fpt
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:one-level-fpt}
Choose $E_{p,D}$ so that $q_{p,D}=p^{E_{p,D}}>Q_{p,D}^2+1$.  Then the single integer
$\nu_{E_{p,D}}(f)$ determines $\operatorname{fpt}(f)$ for every isolated germ with
$\operatorname{Rmod}(f)\le D$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For every principal germ and every $e\ge0$ one has the elementary interval
$\frac{\nu_e(f)}{p^e}\le\operatorname{fpt}(f)\le\frac{\nu_e(f)+1}{p^e}$.  Indeed, the left inequality follows from
the defining Frobenius sequence, while $f^{\nu_e(f)+1}\in\mathfrak m^{[p^e]}$ and Frobenius
iteration give the right inequality.  At $e=E_{p,D}$ the interval has length $\frac{1}{q_{p,D}}$, which is
strictly smaller than the separation in Corollary~\ref{cor:Fjump-separation}.
Theorem~\ref{thm:universal-Fjump-spectrum} therefore leaves exactly
one possible $F$-pure threshold.
head: environment

label: thm:fpt-stratification
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:fpt-stratification}
The modular atlas of Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-modular-classification} can be refined into
finitely many locally closed parameter spaces on which Milnor number, right modality,
and $F$-pure threshold are all constant.  On every irreducible modular family the
$F$-pure threshold is constant on a dense open subset.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $e=E_{p,D}$ and $q=p^e=q_{p,D}$.  For a polynomial family $F(x,t)$, the condition
$F_t^r\in\mathfrak m^{[q]}$ is closed because it is the vanishing of finitely many coefficient
functions after reduction modulo $\langle x_1^q,\ldots,x_n^q\rangle$.  Hence
$\nu_e(F_t)=r$ is locally closed.  Theorem~\ref{thm:one-level-fpt} converts these
finitely many strata into constant-$F$-pure-threshold strata.  On an irreducible
parameter space, one of the finitely many locally closed strata contains the generic
point and therefore contains a dense open subset; this gives the final assertion.
head: environment

label: cor:test-uniform
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Katzman--Lyubeznik--Zhang \cite{KLZ2011} bound the number of jumps by $\operatorname{Tj}(f)+1$.
Since $\operatorname{Tj}(f)\le\mu(f)\le M_{p,D}$, the first assertion follows.  Because $A$ is a reduced hypersurface complete local algebra over the algebraically
closed field $k$, it is absolutely reduced and equidimensional.  Jiang
\cite[Theorem~4.1]{Jiang2021} therefore gives
$\operatorname{Jac}(f)A\subseteq\tau_{\mathrm{fg}}(A)$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:loewy}, applied to the residual germ as in
Proposition~\ref{prop:susp}, gives the displayed power containment; quadratic variables already lie in the Jacobian ideal.  Finally,
\[
 \frac{A}{\operatorname{Jac}(f)A}\cong\frac{R}{\langle f\rangle+\operatorname{Jac}(f)}
\]
is the Tjurina algebra, and $\operatorname{Jac}(f)A\subseteq\tau_{\mathrm{fg}}(A)$ shows that
$\frac{A}{\tau_{\mathrm{fg}}(A)}$ is its quotient.
head: environment

label: cor:finite-BS-sequences
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:finite-BS-sequences}
At fixed $p,D$, only finitely many eventual sequences of level-$e$
positive-characteristic Bernstein--Sato root sets occur for isolated hypersurfaces of right
modality at most $D$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:universal-Fjump-spectrum}, only finitely many numerical $F$-jumping spectra in $(0,1]$ occur at fixed $p,D$. In the non-hyperbolic case, the proof of that theorem replaces the germ, after splitting off its nonsingular quadratic part, by a bounded-degree polynomial in a uniformly bounded number of variables whose localization and completion have the same numerical $F$-jumping spectrum. In the hyperbolic case the spectrum in $(0,1]$ is already fixed. By compatibility of generalized test ideals with completion \cite[Proposition~2.13]{BMS2008}, we may therefore apply Blickle--Stäbler to these polynomial representatives. Their Theorem~5.4 gives, for all sufficiently large $e$, the root set
$\left\{\frac{\lceil\lambda p^e\rceil-1}{p^e}:\lambda\text{ is an }F\text{-jumping number in }(0,1]\right\}$.
Since only finitely many jumping spectra occur, only finitely many eventual level-by-level Bernstein--Sato root sequences occur.
head: environment
